questions.title: How does the Federal Circuit reconcile Fifth Circuit JMOL review with its own "substantial evidence" standard for infringement findings?
questions.question_body: The opinion says denials of JMOL are reviewed de novo under Fifth Circuit law and will be reversed only if the evidence points so overwhelmingly to one side that no reasonable jury could find otherwise. Yet it also says a jury's infringement finding is reviewed for substantial evidence. Practically, which lens controls the outcome here? Are these just two ways of stating the same inquiry on appeal, or is there a distinct two-step analysis (regional-circuit JMOL standard layered over Federal Circuit patent-specific substantial evidence review)?

questions.title: When does contradictory expert testimony require JMOL rather than letting a jury weigh credibility?
questions.question_body: For the '134 patent, the panel held Dr. Wells’s testimony was too confusing/contradictory to support the verdict, citing Johns Hopkins v. Datascope. The district court inferred he actually meant x1/x2 were the claimed signals despite repeated references to the modeled PIM path. What's the line between permissible inference-building by the factfinder and an impermissible attempt to salvage a case with self-contradictory testimony? Is there a doctrinal test or set of factors (e.g., frequency of contradiction, lack of reconciliation, centrality to an element) that triggers reversal?

questions.title: Must the '134 patent's "interference generating signals" be present in the received passband pre-ADC, or can a modeled/derived internal signal qualify?
questions.question_body: The court found no infringement because the accused radios' RF ADC could not have sampled the modeled PIM path—it was generated downstream after sampling. Does the claim language ("over-sampling ... a passband of received signals") categorically require that the 'interference generating signals' be actual received RF content pre-ADC? Could a digitally generated model of PIM ever count as an 'interference generating signal' under this claim, and if not, is that due to claim construction, written description, or just the evidence presented?

questions.title: What exactly must be preserved in a Rule 50(a) motion to avoid waiver of a JMOL theory on appeal?
questions.question_body: The district court deemed AT&T/Nokia to have waived the argument that S1, S2, S3 must be 'unique' because it wasn't raised at Rule 50(a). On appeal, the panel discussed prosecution history and claim scope anyway but reversed on different grounds (insufficient proof of seven multiplications). In practice, how specific must a Rule 50(a) motion be to preserve a claim construction-related noninfringement theory? Is pointing to 'failure of proof on element [d]' enough, or must the party flag the uniqueness point and its legal basis (e.g., disclaimer) to avoid waiver?

questions.title: Did amending from "two or three signals" to "three signals S1, S2, S3" create a prosecution disclaimer against two-unique-signal implementations?
questions.question_body: Appellants argued Finesse surrendered scope by changing 'two or three' to 'three' during prosecution to overcome Filipovic. The panel said no 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal and read the claims as requiring three 'separately identifiable' signals, not necessarily three unique inputs. How is that consistent with the typical inference that narrowing amendments surrender at least some scope? What made this amendment and argument insufficient to constitute disclaimer, and how much weight did the panel give to the distinction between passive vs. active IMPs in assessing scope surrender?

questions.title: How specific must the plaintiff’s mapping be to show the '775 patent’s seven required multiplications are actually performed?
questions.question_body: The Nokia document identified only three distinct multiplications and included modulus and complex conjugate operations. The panel faulted Finesse for not showing that all seven claimed multiplications were performed or explaining any repetition/mapping. What level of evidentiary detail is required to prove a 'seven multiplications' limitation—must the patentee identify each multiplication explicitly, or can they rely on mathematical equivalences/combinations if clearly explained to the jury? Do operations on |x| and x' ever qualify as 'multiplying S1, S2, S3,' and what proof is needed to equate them?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit vacate the damages award instead of rendering judgment of zero after finding noninfringement?
questions.question_body: Given the court reversed the denial of JMOL of noninfringement for all asserted claims, it then 'vacated' the damages award. Is vacatur just the standard label when liability falls away, or does it preserve any possibility of further proceedings on remand (e.g., different claims, different products)? In what scenarios would the Federal Circuit instead enter judgment of zero damages rather than vacate?

questions.title: Was it proper for the district court to rely on inventor testimony to construe S1, S2, S3 as 'separately identifiable' rather than 'unique'?
questions.question_body: The district court's construction leaned on intrinsic evidence and also credited inventor testimony that the three signals 'can be the same signal or different signals.' Under Phillips, extrinsic evidence has limited weight. Was it appropriate to use inventor testimony here, and did the Federal Circuit implicitly endorse that approach by not disturbing the construction? What would have been needed in the intrinsic record to require 'unique' instead?
